utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's happening? I'm hearing French.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't heard you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Yesterday, my team has been doing a great deal to overcome the technical difficulties we experienced yesterday. I believe that we will be able to proceed smoothly today. Your assistants asked that I immediately tender certain exhibits into evidence, and can I do it right now at the outset?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not hear you at all. I have no communication with you whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I was asking: These relate to matters that you have dealt with already in your -- in your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's do that then quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The first exhibit is D00-0078. The second one is DD00-0060. I'm not certain whether the other exhibit was tendered into evidence by the Prosecution, which is the 65 ter document number 2. I see that my learned friends from the Prosecution are nodding, so I do not need to tender this one into evidence. The other one is DD00-0094. Then, 65 ter document 2030. Then 65 ter document 0055.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 2055.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter document number 1. The document dated the 7th of October was, I heard, tendered into evidence by the Prosecution. We have completed the exhibits, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We need to have numbers assigned to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The 65 ter number 1, 00001, was given an exhibit number yesterday when it was admitted, and that will be D1. Number DD000078 becomes Defence Exhibit D2. DD000094 becomes Exhibit D3. 65 ter number 02030 becomes Exhibit D4. And 65 ter number 02055 becomes Exhibit D5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 0060, you did not assign that a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will become Exhibit D6, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, Your Honours -- yesterday, Your Honours, I broke my cross-examination of Mr. Harland - good afternoon to you, Mr. Harland; I apologise for not greeting you beforehand - at the point when we were discussing sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask Mr. Harland to have his statement before him and to read one passage at page 26 of the English version, second paragraph, which is right above the chapter dealing with shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could I ask Mr. Harland to read this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "I am also aware of two instances where the Bosniaks were shooting at Bosniaks. One involved an incident near the Residency in late 1993. The other incident was in early 1994 when General Rose's bodyguard 'Goose' said that he had returned fire on a Bosniak shooting at Bosniaks."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, is that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this, I would like to ask you the following: All the incidents we discussed earlier on, were they, shown in the area where you were in Sarajevo, the result of Serb snipers, representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear or understand the question well. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The incidents, the events where Bosniaks shot upon Bosniaks, as you put it, were they shown in the media to have been the result of sniper fire opened by representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the local media -- I don't know. I don't know. You mean were they --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm also referring to international media, to the media worldwide and the local media in Sarajevo. Were these events always depicted as events caused by representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I understand now. Yes, in general, when there were victims of sniping or shelling within the confrontation lines, that is, on territory controlled by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was normally assumed or presented in the -- at least in the international media, that those firing had been from outside the confrontation lines, that is, from the territory controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska. And that was, in our view, not always the case, though usually the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of this one single instance where the troops of the Army of Republika Srpska shot at their own civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had no knowledge of any incidents of that sort. We didn't have good access, but I would also doubt if there were any such incidents. Can I make a slight --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. The witness wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I wanted to make a slight clarification, which is we were aware of incidents in which, on the Serb side of the line, one Serb might have been targeted or killed by another, but that was of a different nature. That was when one group was conflicting with another. So I just wanted to make that clarification, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand well, these were typical murders which were the result of relations between persons such as occur throughout the world. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either criminal or political differences, yes. More normal, you might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement - and I don't think there's any need for me to identify the paragraph; I'm sure you remember this - you talked about both sides engaging in certain sniping activities wherein there was an exchange of fire between snipers, in other words, soldiers --

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- from one side would shoot at soldiers from the other side, and they were snipers.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you've confirmed this, this means that both sides indeed had to have snipers for military purposes --

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- provided that they did not abuse them?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have finished with the sniping topic. I would like to move on to another topic briefly. In late December - I suppose you're aware of this - the former president of the United States of America, Jimmy Carter, was in Sarajevo. Thanks to him and to the negotiations he brokered, a peace -- a truce agreement was reached that lasted between January and April, that's to say, four months.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't wish to inquire about the details concerning the agreement. I don't think there's any need for that at the moment, not even to discuss the events that took place at the time. At any rate, this agreement was different from all the previous ones; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, we called it even by a different name. We called it a comprehensive cessation of hostilities agreement. Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on to a matter connected with some issues we discussed yesterday that I have to go back to in order to highlight matters that I believe are relevant in view of Mr. Milosevic's defence. Yesterday, you said that it was in the autumn of 1994, or rather, up until that point Serbs actually wanted the situation surrounding Sarajevo to be crystallised and that they ceased all fire by the autumn of 1994, at least reduced the fire. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Next we spoke of the anti-sniping agreement, which, in your assessment, yielded results that spanned over several months.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At that point, several days before the end of summer, on the 18th of September, incidents occurred - if you recall, we discussed them - and another one on the 2nd of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something concerning an event we did not discuss and which took place at the end of October 1994, namely, the events taking place at Igman in the demilitarised zone. Do you recall that event?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would not go into the details concerning the event. This is a military issue, after all, and we will have to discuss the matter at a later stage. Do you recall that quite a few Serb soldiers were killed in the process and that medical nurses and medical staff who were going to help the wounded and to rescue some people were killed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the incident and I also recall that some medical staff were killed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, Muslims, the soldiers of the Bosnian army, took control of Igman. After the Serbs had fully demilitarised the area, the Muslim army seized the opportunity and captured Igman. If you do wish to confirm this, please say so; if not, then explain why not.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were two separate processes going on. You are correct that in 1993 the Serb forces had controlled Mount Igman and they agreed to withdraw, and they did withdraw. Subsequent to that, forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina sometimes transited the area in violation of the agreement in order to make attacks on Serb positions beyond the demilitarised zone, and the incident which you referred to just now, sir, I believe, is in that category. The separate question of whether they re-occupied the zone, the demilitarised zone itself, that was also something which occurred, though it occurred slowly, over a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From that point on, after that incident, or over these several days, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina held the positions at Igman.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it took place over a series of many months. The incident you are referring to, I believe, actually took place outside the demilitarised zone, but it is certainly true that the Bosnian forces got to that point by transiting through the demilitarised zone, which was a violation of the Igman agreement of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to be more precise than that. Can you tell us at what time was it that the soldiers of BH army captured Igman, took up positions there, and had the commanding view and control over Sarajevo, when was that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, they tended not to directly control areas of the demilitarised zone of Igman. What they did was they transited through the zone and then controlled points just beyond the zone, so that the whole of the zone de facto came under their -- under their control. And that was a process which happened gradually. I believe the -- I don't remember the exact date, but the agreement was made sometime in the autumn of 1993. I was there with Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic and later with General Delic and President Izetbegovic. And the violations by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina began almost immediately, but they didn't secure control of the whole area by establishing points beyond it until the end of 1994, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But it happened at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We were trying to overcome difficulties with the equipment that we are using, and I hope that I have mastered it. We have DD00-0127 in front of us now. This is a report by the UNPROFOR staff in Sarajevo for the entire month of December. I have page 3 in the English version. I think I've cited the correct number.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure my screen is on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm told there is a technical difficulty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah-ha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, it's here now. It's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At page 3 of the English version, "Sector Sarajevo," the total exclusion zone in Sarajevo, it says: "Nothing to report." And then it says: "This situation in the Sector Sarajevo was relatively quiet on the 1st of December." Did you see this report before and can you confirm that this is, indeed, what it says?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot, after these years, confirm that I've seen this report before, but it certainly looks like a real document. And in general, these sector reports were very accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just for everybody's ease, the relevant part is just at the bottom of this page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah-ha --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- B, if it could be scrolled down. Now we can see Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is about the Sagger missiles. I remember that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was just this one point that I read out that was relevant for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But that is not what was on the screen, so we have to be grateful to Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In any event, it's there now and you have the witness's answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, except there's a question as to whether we're discussing one incident, which is clearly a Bosnian violation, or the incident at the bottom, which is clearly a Serb violation --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Item number 2 --

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- Mr. Witness, I wanted to deal with it in general terms. It says here: "The situation in Sector Sarajevo was quiet and relatively calm."

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, I'm interested in what we can read at page 5 of the English version, the part concerning the assessment of UNPROFOR intelligence. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: D.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: For Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. First comes Croatia, and number 2 is Sarajevo. And I am going to read to you subitem B, which reads: "The continual bringing in of troops of Bosnia-Herzegovina into the area west of the Ilijas salient," number so-and-so, "suggests that the BH are either stiffening their defensive posture in the area or possibly preparing for a renewal of offensive operations." Is that true, and were you aware of that at that time; or is this correct, what is stated in this report?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, what is stated in the report; yes, I was aware of it at the time; and yes, it was part of a broader build-up by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to attempt to break out of the siege of Sarajevo in the spring of 1995. Yes, sir, all three.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later on we can read what you just said, that they were preparing themselves. There is another thing in this report. On page 7 of the English version, Sector East, Sector South, and then comes Sector Sarajevo. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Subitem A reads: "Shots were fired from a BH position at FreBat's observation point." Is this correct? Was that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Under B, subitem B: "A BH soldier in Butmir threw a hand-grenade at the French APC." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And subitem C: "A rifle grenade from ABiH position was fired on the Russian observation point." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would be grateful if we can have on our monitors a part of the transcript from the Slobodan Milosevic trial when Mr. Harland gave evidence, page 26961, lines 11 to 18. I hope there's not another misunderstanding here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there a problem, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm informed that the e-court procedures require that the Defence or a party publish any document that the party wishes to use, so that it is your responsibility to have that document put on the screen; it's not the registrar's.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I made a great effort yesterday to facilitate our proceedings today, both for you and myself, and I was told yesterday I cannot -- I will probably manage to overcome this. But yesterday I operated in that way, and I know that Mr. Harland was able to see the transcript and his evidence that he gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me ask the Prosecutor whether he is in a position to assist; if not, then you'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can assist in two ways. We have the 65 ter number of the two transcripts, so I think it could be brought up. That's 2815 or 2816. And because it is the first day, I think it's 2815. Yes, I think we have it now. I do also have a hard copy, if we need, which could be put on to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand it's Prosecution Exhibit number 1 in this case. In future, Mr. Tapuskovic, know where the responsibility lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall take a very good note of this, and rest assured that this will not happen again. I've wasted lots of time so far. Are we on this page? Lines 11 to 18, the literal translation is: "... The defence position adopted that time was on their side. Until 1995, a sufficient quantity -- enough weapons were getting to the Bosnian government and the relations between the Bosnian government and the Bosnian Croats had improved to such a degree that there was a real military threat from the Bosnian government for the first time, and of course the Bosnian government actually had a numerical advantage in troop strength over the Serbs, and the Serbs became anxious of that." Is this, more or less, what you said on that occasion and is that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I said that and it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to clarify just one issue. You said enough weapons, so in addition to numerical strength, they also were at an advantage with the weapons over the opposing side.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a large number of weapons flowing by that time to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so their troops were better armed. They never got the heavy weapons or the tanks, but by this stage they had almost enough light weapons to arm, we estimated, perhaps about 200.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Elsewhere you said -- let us not go back to it again because it will take up much more time than I can afford, and I will skip that in order to expedite my cross-examination. The next document is 65 ter number 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I hate to interrupt my learned friend, and also I hate to suggest that he does something procedurally, but I believe before going to the Milosevic transcript, this UNPROFOR document, dated 1st December 1994, was discussed, and that's the number 10 on the bundle received from the Defence. So I suggest that if the Defence moves to have it admitted into evidence, it should be done now before moving on to the next exhibit. That's just my observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Naturally, I intend to move this 65 ter 10 document to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted. Please give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit Number D6 -- 7, Your Honours, sorry. D7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a report dated the 30th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have it in front of you? On page 1 of this report we see in a Mr. Akashi, General Smith, and General Javier had a meeting with the Bosnian government officials, and it says that the Bosnian Serbs had reiterated their offer to extend the agreement from April for an indefinite period of time. Was that true and correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe -- I was not at this meeting, but that was the -- that was the position, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On page 1, also under item 2, we see that Mr. Akashi, General Smith, and General Javier also had talks with Silajdzic, and it is stated here that Silajdzic, as far as the extension of the cessation of hostilities agreement, confirmed that it was not in their interest for this agreement to be extended and he refused to discuss it. Was that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I was not at that meeting, but certainly the Bosnians were --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says here in the document.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, and I believe it's true, because the Bosnians were preparing an offensive at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters for interrupting the witness while he was giving the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Under item 5 of this same document, or on page 2 of the English version, it says under item 5 Mr. Akashi proposed that the agreement on the cessation of hostilities be either extended or renewed. Is that also true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I have to say I was not at this meeting, but that generally reflects the Bosnian view, that a stabilisation of the situation around Sarajevo was not in their interests and that they would prepare an offensive during the spring of 1995. So I believe that this document is almost certainly a correct reflection of what was said at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters can barely hear the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the interpreters are having difficulty hearing you. So what is he to do, to speak more directly into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Obviously something is wrong with the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to bow a little, although I find it difficult. But if necessary, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we don't wish to affect your posture, but let's try again and see. I'd like to ask the technical staff to have a look at the microphone, but we'll continue until that is done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that the paper that I'm holding in front of the microphone is making a noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Harland --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It may very well be the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, I have a document that you drafted dated the 24th of June, 1995, and you sent it to Phillip, I think it is, Corwin, the last name. I can't see it clearly. Do you have it? This is 65 ter 471.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I move for this document also to be tendered into evidence, 65 ter 2471.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it. And please assign a number to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have it in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you may have used two other documents without seeking to tender them as exhibits; if that is so, then let's have all of them tendered. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I believe there is only one. That's the one the witness has just been discussing, the 30th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit that. Please give that a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D8.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So this is a report of yours, if you have it in front of you, dated the 24th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "No" meaning it's not in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not in front of me, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not in front of me either. What's the position there, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am told that your case manager's mouse is not functioning and that appears to be the root of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What I can assist with, Mr. President, is the 65 ter number of this document would be 2471.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 2471. Then perhaps the registrar can assist. We're having birthing pains with this e-court system.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh. It has given birth. Yeah. This is a document by me, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of the English version, paragraph 3 reads: "BH army attacked on the 15th and 16th of June Serbian position all along the confrontation line ..." Was that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I don't have the -- oh, yeah, yeah, the paragraph 2 -- yes, that was a failed Bosnian -- quite a large Bosnian offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you later about this. Can you just confirm whether this was true, because the next document speaks about this. But this is what it reads here, what I just read to you, and I'm asking you, is this true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that I wrote this document and yes, it's true that those events happen. I sometimes don't know which one you're asking when you say "is it true?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I read out to you and what is contained in your report. Is that yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I think you can easily answer this.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes is the answer because it's the answer to both, but sometimes you seem to be asking me: Is that what is written, or is what is written true? And in this case the answer is definitely yes because both are true. But it would help me if you could clarify. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You're right. I should have formulated it more clearly. I wouldn't dwell longer on these issues, but three passages or paragraphs down, there is a very short sentence which reads: "On the 23rd of June," which means only eight days after the beginning of the offensive, the Serbs had asked for 500 body-bags from your civil affairs office. Was that correct or true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move that this document be tendered into evidence as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it. Yes, please give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As number D9, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The next document is another report of yours dated the 2nd of July addressed to Phillip Corwin; 65 ter 2503. Do you have it in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 2 July, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On page 1, the summary or highlights reads what you just said a while ago. You said that "the Bosnian offensive around Sarajevo spatters on without any conspicuous success. Ground taken by the Bosnians seems to have been re-taken by the Serbs." Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the offensive collapsed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have the documents enlarged as soon as they are put on the screen, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is English version page 2, and you reiterated this, and then you spoke of some -- about some other things. But you say here: "On Wednesday, 28th June, the Bosnians attempted another attack out of the city." Was that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you went on to say that: "The attack came from the western part of the town and was focussed on ... Nedzarici," which you showed on the map yesterday. Was that also true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "The nearby areas of Stup and Rajlovac were also attacked." This was also true; yes?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "The operation seems to have failed and the Serbs may even have succeeded in pushing the Bosnians back in Stup." This was also true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it appeared to us at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After that, it reads: "The Bosnian media - which had been boasting of 'newly liberated territories' - is now talking of the army's 'heroic defence' of the city." Was this also true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm particularly interested to hear from you whether this was also true or not, and on page 3, which reads as follows. In this paragraph, above "Location of Bosnian Weapons," you say that: "UNPROFOR retaliated with 120-millimetre mortars it has placed on Mount Igman," and that they were firing at the Serbs. Was this true as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are UNPROFOR mortars we're talking about now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you this is as follows: The next heading: "Location of Bosnian Weapons," and I would also like to check whether this is true, and I'm asking you: Is it true that, as you say here: "Since the Bosnian offensive began two weeks ago, the number of Bosnian heavy weapons operating near UNPROFOR facilities has significantly increased."

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everything in this document is true as I understood it at the time. And if I may say so, the point of this document is, of course, when they defeated the Bosnians militarily, they began an indiscriminate bombardment of the city and sniping against civilians. So we don't even need perhaps to go paragraph by paragraph. Everything in the document I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What you just said is not in your report. I do appreciate that you have the right to say it --

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's in this document. Can we please go to the very summary of this document. I feel you're really misrepresenting this document we have in front of us. Can we see the top, just the cover the cover page. It says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear from Mr. Tapuskovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have nothing against Mr. Harland's saying something after I finished my presentation, and the point is in this paragraph, and probably this is why Mr. Harland reacted in this way. I do understand him. He may think that he is allowed to say what he wishes to say, but before that I would like him to confirm this paragraph for the record because this is the crux of the matter and the point of this whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe he has already confirmed it. Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He has just asked what the point of the whole document is. Well, I would tell him that the point of the whole document is what is written in paragraph 1 on the front page. If we can see it again, it summarises all that goes after, which says: The Bosnians attempted a military break-out of the city, they were militarily defeated by the Serbs, and in retaliation the Serbs then undertook what we considered to be an indiscriminate bombardment of the civilian population and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, that would more properly be a point taken up in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I just didn't want the document misrepresented. It's there in paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think what the witness took offence of is the fact that Mr. Tapuskovic said, what you just said was not in the report, and that's what triggered Mr. Harland's point. And this comment by Mr. Tapuskovic was at line 23 and that's the reaction of the witness when he said, "No, that's not true, it is in the report and it was on page 1," as Mr. Harland confirmed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic -- I did take offence at that when he said there was not something in the report which clearly was in the report from paragraph 1. I also was not happy when he said that what the whole point of the report was - that was his words - what was the point of the report. I mean, I wrote the report, I know what the point of it was. The point of it was the indiscriminate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, just a minute. In answer to Mr. Tapuskovic's question about the point of the report, you made a reference to paragraph 1, so I'd like to see paragraph 1 now because it's a matter that was raised by Mr. Tapuskovic. May we have a look at paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, the Serbs have resumed a more or less indiscriminate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you just summarise it for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it says here: "The Bosnian offensive around Sarajevo sputters on without any conspicuous success." Later: "The Serbs have resumed more or less indiscriminate bombardment of the city. Snipers are active. Civilian casualties are high." And so when he tells me the point of the document is something else, I can say I wrote the document and the point of it is what I have just read and is stated in paragraph 1, that the Serb military retaliation was against civilians causing high numbers of civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Chairman, I think that -- I feel something that the witness is actually proving right now. I have nothing against your technique and this e-court, but when Defence and the Prosecutor is giving us a document on e-court, we're only shown the one paragraph or a couple of paragraphs. And I would have wanted to have the entire text in order to see also the other paragraphs, maybe the third -- the second or the third page. So this is what I suggest. I don't know if it's simple, I don't know if it's too expensive for case managers and both parties, but couldn't they give us a hard copy of the documents that were shown and maybe give a copy -- a hard copy also to the witness. I'm sure that would help. That way we could follow what's going on, otherwise it's too complicated. We see only one paragraph, we don't see the other paragraphs, we don't have a full idea, a full picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I am misrepresented by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You needn't worry about the misrepresentation because your counsel has a right to raise the matter in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Since it arose from a point raised by way of question, I allowed you to look at paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe just a point to respond. I'm also not an expert. I am not an expert in e-court, but I understand that Your Honours have the ability to, in fact, look at each document yourself and you can scroll through the other pages. That's what I'm being told by an expert on e-court. But perhaps we can raise it in a different setting when we have more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll continue. Continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really have no intention to abuse the document. I've read this sentence and I know what it means, and I know that this was done merely by way of introduction. I may have made an error, but I was interested in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the provocations and the Bosnian weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, at page 3 where you said: "Since the Bosnian offensive began two weeks ago, the number of Bosnian heavy weapons operating from near UNPROFOR facilities has significantly increased." This is something you wrote and, first of all, can you confirm that this is indeed what the text says?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will confirm that's what --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me to confirm what the text says. The text is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will read on for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can be heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think there's no need to cut off the witness. Sometimes it's just not possible to say yes or no, and I think the Defence has enough time. We don't object, you know, that this is being done in a polite manner. I'm not suggesting it's not, but please can the witness be allowed to finish his sentences. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. His technique, Mr. Harland, is to ask you first if that is what the text says and then I think he's going to go on to ascertain whether the contents are true.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, that's what half the text says. And for me, as the person who observed the events and then wrote the report, to take one paragraph which says that Bosnian heavy weapons are located near UNPROFOR facilities has increased, without the other half of the text, which gives the context, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But then you have a right --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- to put it in context --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good. Ah. Well, I want to exercise it but I get -- keep getting told just to say yes or no. And all I would say is I -- if you read the next paragraph, it says UNPROFOR was unable to determine whether this was an effort by the Bosnians to draw counter-battery fire from the Serbs or whether it was just a function of the general increase in the number of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let Mr. Tapuskovic continue his questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, Mr. President, I've lost a great deal of time discussing this matter and I was wrong in not just reading this one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, Mr. Harland, it reads: "Some people in UNPROFOR see this as an effort by the Bosnians to draw counter-battery fire on to UNPROFOR, which would then be drawn into conflict with the Serbs." Is that exactly what it says? Please answer my question. You've only nodded.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what one sentence says. There is one more sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will read it for you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Others note that there has been an increase in the number of active weapons and that the density of heavy weapons is not greater around UNPROFOR facilities than it is elsewhere." Was this accurately reported?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is my next question: Does this mean that not only were there heavy weapons within the UNPROFOR building or facilities, but also around it, elsewhere, in the vicinity of UNPROFOR facilities and elsewhere in Sarajevo? Hence my question.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender the document into evidence. I believe that this is 65 ter 2503 and the most important document for the Defence so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Will the registrar please give it a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's already D9. It's already admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The most recent check shows that it's already admitted as a Prosecution Exhibit P19.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, in your evidence - and we're looking for it in the transcript - concerning the Markale 2 incident - and this was your evidence in the Slobodan Milosevic case - you stated in connection with this something which I would like you to read out now. I do not wish to enter into an argument about this with you. This is at page 28670, line 22. It's just several lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not on my screen either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, that should be Prosecution Exhibit number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. Now, we have it on the screen, but we need to find the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 22, at page 28670. The next one is 28671, which is an empty page because of the need to repaginate it with the French version, and then page 28672, line -- lines 1 to 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If the witness has found the bit, can he please read it out.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which line, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, 28670 is the page, and the line is 22.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In all cases which I could speak about - I mean we could go through them one by one at great length - are either certainly fired from the Serb side or it's unclear."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you wish him to go further?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The text goes on to say that: "The one we are discussing is one of the unclear ones. When it comes to Markale 2, I believe the case to be less unclear. But I think I have nothing to add on this one. It was unclear."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this your statement? Is this what you stated in evidence?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is what I stated, and I would perhaps like to clarify that it's unclear in the sense that there's some doubt, but frankly not very much doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The 65 ter document 481, the English version thereof, at page 3. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sector Sarajevo. You talk about the fact that on that day five shells landed. I don't think there's any need for me to read this through, but there is this one sentence here.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it. I have some other page of what I think is the right document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can it be put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 3 of the English version. UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Five mortar shells landed. That's there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you the following: Several lines down it says: "It is very difficult to establish the position from which mortar shells were fired because it is impossible to determine the level of charge used to fire the projectiles." This was written in the first report on the 28th. Are you aware of this or not? Although, having been written here, it should be correct.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a first report. The commanding officer, General Smith, asked for a technical team to review it, and I was present in the room when that technical team from our intelligence, our G2 cell, made their report. And in my physical presence, they said that the -- the shells, the mortar bombs, that killed these 30 people and injured these 80 others, had been fired from Serb positions in Lukavica. They said that was beyond doubt. In the final written report of the G2 - it's a confidential document, but it seems to have made its way to this court somehow - it is qualified, it is beyond reasonable doubt. So when I have said in my testimony that there is some unclarity, this is an unclear case, I would prefer to be recorded that I agree with the G2 assessment that it is beyond reasonable doubt that these shells which caused these civilian casualties were fired from the Serb side and deliberately at a crowded market, if I can say, if one can guess at their motive. Can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is your comment. I do not wish to go into that. I do not wish to challenge what you're saying right now. I'd like to know the following: Do you know that the senior officer, Mr. Demurenko, who has been mentioned here several times, on that day - and I had footage of that but there's no need for me to show it to you - he stated that the possibility that this arrived from Serb positions was 1:1.000.000. Are you aware of this statement of his?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: He made a statement which was deemed by the technical team, the expert team, to be factually incorrect. The technical team which reviewed it found Colonel Demurenko's statement very unconvincing because it was based on the ballistic signature of one of the five mortar bombs. All four of the other mortar bombs showed the same ballistic signature which indicated a firing point around Lukavica. The fact that one mortar bomb showed a different ballistic signature is consistent with the fact that that bomb, mortar bomb, on its impact, either came through a tiled roof or hit a table on the way down. So Mr. Demurenko's views were stated at the time. They were stated outside of the context of a credible technical investigation. So, yes, I am aware of them, and that is one of the reasons I have said that there is some doubt. But can I say, because this is a rather important moment in the history of the war, that the principal doubt about who fired these five mortar shells that killed all these civilians arises because General Smith made a statement to the press that his investigation showed that it was not clear who fired the shells. Now, in fact, I had been speaking with General Smith, and he chose to make that very neutral statement when, in fact, he was already aware - he had in his hand the technical assessment - that the shots were fired from Lukavica. He chose to make a neutral statement so as to not to alarm the Serbs, who would otherwise have known that he was about to call in NATO air-strikes, which is what, in fact, he did. So, in my view, this Markale 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And how would you know that that was why he made this neutral statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was advising him to do that. I was with him that morning. The situation, Your Honour, was that when it was reported that the Serbs had fired these rounds and killed this large number of civilians, he decided, on the advice of his colleagues, that he would call for widespread NATO air attacks. The problem that he had was that at that very moment some UNPROFOR troops, British troops, were on Serb-held territory between Gorazde and the Serbian border. He, therefore, needed a few hours of time to get the UNPROFOR troops off Serb territory to be entirely safe before the NATO bombers could be brought in. And so, I spoke with him about it and I advised that he make a fairly neutral statement. And it has been a cause of distress to me for more than a decade that this neutral statement has given rise to a mythology that there is any real serious doubt that the -- that the Serbs fired these rounds, when we have a very clear technical report that they did. I believe it's even in the documents in this case somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier on you said exactly what you've repeated now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. The question which I asked has not been accurately reflected. I asked: How would you know that that was why he made a neutral statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking again. I'm asking that the question be properly reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, today you said three times that the shell flew in from Lukavica, according to your knowledge. The indictment alleges that the shell flew in from Trebevic, the highest mount above Sarajevo. How do you account for that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am willing to stand corrected on the firing point, if that's what the G2 report says, but the G2 -- the UNPROFOR G2 intelligence technical assessment report that was presented to General Smith in my presence clearly indicated that it came -- the five rounds, beyond reasonable doubt, came from points in Serb-held territory. If the grid references were not locations near Lukavica, then I apologise. I may have erred in that, but I have certainly not erred in the conclusion. And if that document is in this court, I would simply, obviously, be guided by that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have almost completed my cross-examination; however, at the outset we were dealing with some other matters and then we had some discussions and some technical difficulties. I would need some additional time to complete the three remaining topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much time would that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hopefully within 20 minutes I would finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time for the break now, so we'll break for 20 minutes and we'll give you the 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Since we were on the subject of Markale 2 and the events relating to it, I'll try as quickly as possible to finalise this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, General Smith, on that very same day, on the 28th, issued certain orders or submitted certain reports. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was the 28th or the 29th I now don't recall, but certainly by the -- by the 29th, General Smith had decided to turn the key that would activate NATO air attacks against the Bosnian Serb army, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I may be mistaken, but I noted down that it was on the 28th. But nevertheless I do accept what you just said. After that, the following day, NATO bombing began. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I remember correctly, but obviously it's a matter of easy historical record, I thought that the bombing began on the night between the 29th and the 30th, not on the night between the 28th and the 29th, and -- because I remember General Smith asked me to call Dr. Karadzic to tell him that the attacks were about to begin and that -- and what the reason was. But I thought that was on the evening of the 29th, but it's a very long time ago now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I may be mistaken. Since you were the representative of the UN, the bombing began without the decision of the Security Council, and that was the first NATO bombing in its history of that kind.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bombing began in accordance with the procedure established between NATO and the United Nations, the so-called dual-key process, dual-key arrangement. One key for the launching of the bombing resided with the United Nations, and that key was turned by General Smith in the period either -- I think on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This was turned in favour of NATO or was it NATO's decision?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dual-key arrangement required that both the United Nations and NATO should agree, should so-call turn the key, before NATO air attacks could begin. NATO's key was turned by others and was not our immediate concern. Actually, I believe the NATO key was held by Admiral Layton Smith in Naples, but that was not our concern. Our concern was whether we would turn our key, and that decision rested with the United Nations under this agreement between the two organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For about two weeks these NATO strikes were very fierce.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the intention, and it was also accompanied by a major bombardment of Serb positions around Sarajevo by the UNPROFOR Rapid Reaction Force on Mount Igman. I believe that, just on the first night, we fired many hundreds of shells to try and suppress the artillery fire of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Quite a few aerial bombs. Would it be fair to say that they're never too accurate and that quite a few civilian casualties were sustained as a result of these aerial bombs being dropped?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, of course, the Serbs were very quick to protest to us when we had inflicted any casualties, or even when the Bosnians had inflicted any casualties on them in violation of any of the agreements. And in the period following the bombardment by our artillery and the air attacks, we did not receive reports of substantial casualties. And the battle damage assessment photography did not give us the impression that there were civilian casualties. The targets were chosen quite precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did they hit the targets precisely?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, NATO aircraft were in operation and attacking targets which, on the whole, they had identified, so I cannot speak very well for NATO. Our artillery certainly was under our command and control. But once the key was turned, under this dual-key arrangement, there was substantial freedom of action, including in target selection, that then rested with NATO. But our understanding was that the targets were chosen in a way to minimise civilian casualties and that, in fact, they had. For example, one of the principal targets we were very concerned about was that we wanted to destroy the bridge over the Drina at Foca in order to prevent reinforcements from Yugoslavia, and the battle damage photos show that the bridge had been completely destroyed without touching any of the surrounding area, so we were quite confident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to hear about the civilian-populated areas and whether there were any casualties there. Very well. What I heard from you will suffice. Do you know what the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina provided or fed very precise and accurate data about the Serbian positions concerning troops and weapons? Daily reports were filed by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to NATO, and subsequently NATO engaged those targets. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know about that, and I can't believe it. But in general, I think that our information was more accurate than theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know - or maybe you don't know - that the BH army at one point also procured 800 aerial bombs?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems strange because they had no aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't have any aircraft, but they could have been used in a different way. I wouldn't like to tackle this issue any longer. Do you know that prior to these events, 26 aircraft with very serious weaponry was received by BH army?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean they received 26 fixed-wing aircraft in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Twenty-six aircraft, yes. According to Alija Izetbegovic and his address to the Presidency - I have this document; I will very soon present it to this Chamber - in a discussion with Silajdzic, he said that in those days they had received 26 aircraft. That's what he said. And you know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had some -- they had some helicopters, a small number of helicopters, and they had a couple of very light spotter aircraft. They had no combat aircraft operating over the theatre; that was one of their main problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have been cautioned that my question was about the weapons transported in aircrafts, whereas the translation was about equipment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Yes, you are right. Aircraft were delivering weapons to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; that is correct. I'm sorry, I misunderstood your question, or it was perhaps misinterpreted, I don't know, as understanding that actual aircraft had been delivered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Indeed, that is what is reflected in the transcript, so I'm grateful for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now move on to the last two topics. During the break, with your assistance, I tried to locate the pages that I would like to refer to in my examination of Mr. Harland. First of all, it's 28642, line 10; that's the transcript from the Slobodan Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you can see it in front of you. In your evidence you explained earlier that due to the fact that you were staying in the Muslim-controlled part of Sarajevo, you were unable to say much about the casualties sustained by the army or the civilians on the Serbian side when the cease-fire agreement was being violated because the Serbs did not allow you - or journalists, for that matter - to move freely around the area under their control.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We had much better information about casualties and military activity on the Bosnian side of the line, where we had a much heavier presence. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But UNPROFOR had much more observation points on the positions of the Serbian side, some 11 of them, as far as I know; and on the Bosnian side there were only three. So there were much more observation positions from which you could have seen what was happening on the Serbian side. Did you ever receive any reports from them about the casualties sustained on the Serbian side, both among the troops and among the civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it's not correct that we had more observation posts on the Serb side than on the Bosnian side. We had many more observation posts on the Bosnian side. Also, on the Bosnian side, we had access to the morgue and to the hospitals usually, not always, and also we were present in the civilian-inhabited areas, whereas most of the observation positions we had that looked on to Serb positions were generally not in densely inhabited areas. We had one position in Debelo Brdo, which we discussed on our first day, which I think you could, at a distance, look down into Grbavica. But in general, for civilian casualties on the Serb side, we generally had to wait for the Serbs to tell us that there had been civilian casualties. We often wanted to confirm this by seeing bodies, and they would usually refuse us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have already explained that. What I wanted to hear is whether you, as a civilian observer - and on the Serbian side there were quite a few hospitals - did you ever visit any of the Serbian hospitals to see whether there were any wounded people there, wounded civilians, or ...

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, they would not let us most of the time. Often we would get protests --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in which they would say somebody was at a hospital or their hospital ran out of electricity. But when we asked to check - General Mladic made this allegation several times - we were refused permission. So usually we didn't have access.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have already explained that. The next paragraph, 28699, that's the page number, lines 8 to 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have three minutes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask you, I have one more topic, Your Honours, to cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the Chamber has been more than generous in its allocation of time to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sure that you have been very tolerant, but would you please just take into consideration that it has been very difficult over the past two days to overcome all these technical difficulties. I only have one topic left. I will finish and wrap up very quickly, pose brief questions, and therefore conclude my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, as this is the first witness, yes. But how much longer do you anticipate? Not more than ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best, Your Honours. I have one more topic and one more question, and then I'll conclude. Thank you very much. I think it will be all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you can just give me a quick and short answer. Can you see this page, 28699, in front of you --

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- lines 8 to 14? You say here - and unfortunately at the time I was questioning you as an amicus curiae - that the Muslims provoked very often by returning fire and this happened quickly -- particularly in Sarajevo. They behaved in that way in order to attract the attention of the media. You explained that the Muslims wanted the media to see the Serbs while they were attacking, and sometimes they created conditions for that to be perceived. You also know that it happened on rare occasions in other parts of the country where the media were not -- had not so much influence. That's what you basically said. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I said was what is stated here in the transcript from 10 to 14, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last topic. In order to be able to ask any questions, can we just scroll a few lines. If you can read it yourself, it will be much easier. Page 28659, line 1, and page 28658, lines 24 and 25. Can you please read it yourself.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lines 24 and 25?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 24 and 25, and the next line on the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "There certainly had been Serbs from Sarajevo killed and their bodies put in the pits of Kazani, above Bistrik barracks, and ..." here my page ends, "and that the people who did it were certainly associated with Caco." His Honour mentioned that I can clarify, if I may, some of the context. If I can say, I did indeed say that when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll allow the witness, Mr. Tapuskovic, to give a clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the overwhelming number of Serbs who were killed within the confrontation lines, that is, on Bosnian-held territory, were killed by Serb gun-fire. And when Mr. Milosevic, in the context of that trial, people wanted to know if there were any exceptions to that, I said yes, there were some exceptions, and this Kazani incident with Caco was one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also said - and I must read this now in French because I don't have time to have it translated - "Caco was a dangerous man."

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember if I said that, but he was certainly a dangerous man, yes. I don't have the lines, but, yes, that sounds a very plausible thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you went on to say: "At the end of October 1940 -- 1993 -- at the end of October 1993" -- I believe this is what you said, that you believed that he was killed in October 1993 by his own men.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, not by his subordinates. I think he was killed by the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, though in fact I think -- Caco, of course, had not only been killing Serbs; he had been killing Muslims as well. And I think, in fact, the action which led to his own death was a last spasm of violence in which he had killed a number of Muslims, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you did say that he had killed several dozen people and that it was shocking at the time when you were there. Is that correct? And Caco was not the only one. He had a whole unit that was engaged in that. He didn't do it on his own. His whole unit was doing that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: His whole unit was engaged in violence; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: He was murdered in order not to testify to what he did or to be tried for the crimes that he committed against the Serbs of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- excuse me, sir, I'm not sure of which document you are quoting from. The French that you read out, where is that from?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. The English version, page 28659, lines 15 to 25; and page 28611 -- 661, lines 1 to and 6 and lines 1 to 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's the Milosevic transcript; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anyway, my answer is: No, I do not think that is why he was killed. I think he was killed because he had not subordinated himself to the authorities of the Bosnian government and that he was at the time of his death, in fact, taking violent action against some of the Bosnian government people. And I think it is certainly true that as he killed Serbs, he also killed Muslims; but I think that, more importantly, it's -- it's true that the great majority of Serbs who were killed on Bosnian territory were killed by gun-fire from the Serb side of the line, not by Caco.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Microphone for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Around 300 people were killed by artillery fire, but I will not go into that any further. Mr. Milosevic asked you about this, and you responded that the figure of 8 to 9.000 was exaggerated, that it was absolutely not true. Now, we already have documents prepared by some NGOs and other institutions and organisations; some of them have been provided for certain cases tried before this Tribunal. When all of that started in 1992, do you know that between 2 and 3.000 Serbs - and there are names of these people - were killed and slaughtered and thrown into Kazani? And my question is: Do you know anything about? Tell me just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I believe that's completely untrue. In fact -- no, no, no, clear -- that is a gross misrepresentation of the facts. We kept quite accurate records of the people who died or who went missing or whose families reported them missing, and it would be a grotesque exaggeration to say that between 8 or 9.000 Serbs had been killed, or even that 2 or 3.000 Serbs had been killed. It was certainly less than 1.000, and by our examinations, the overwhelming majority of them were killed by gun-fire, sniping, or shelling directed at civilians from the Serb side of the line. So what you say is simply not correct, and I don't know what the NGO is but you should use a different source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what if you are correct that between 2 and 3.000 Serbs were killed? What is the point that you would be making in relation to that? What is your case in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask the following, and this is my last question. I don't want to belabour the point because somebody might accuse me of tu quoque --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm entitled to try to ascertain what your case is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
