utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I will answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there greater fear among the Serbs with regard to the bombs that were landing in Sarajevo because they could have sought shelter or was there fear among them because on that day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I asked you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've asked me why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this was important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I asked -- yes. Why is it important to your case that 2 or 3.000 Serbs were killed, and you haven't answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbs feared that this should happen to them anywhere where Muslims were in control. There was everyday fear among them, that any day someone would come and collect them and throw them in pits in Kazani, and this fear was far greater than the rest and it dominated everything else. It so happened that people were taken out of their homes, never to return again, and some of them are known to have been killed and thrown into pits. There was talk about them being very few and that's not true. Mr. Harland himself spoke about under a thousand of them --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How would that affect the liability of Mr. Milosevic for the crimes with which he's charged?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the reasons why they had a stronghold on their positions was that should it so happen that places where they resided would be taken over, the same thing would happen to them as was happening to the Serbs. Because in the area of responsibility of Republika Srpska in Sarajevo, of the 1st Corps, not a single person met his or her end this way. And I didn't have time to ask him whether he knew of camps, of the silos camp. Could the gentleman please finally explain what was happening at the silos camp in 1995, and let this be my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. First, in reply to your half-asked question about the fear of the Serbs in Sarajevo, my experience of the Serbs in Sarajevo is that most of them wished -- or many of them wished to leave the city of Sarajevo but were unable to do so. And the reason they wanted to leave was because the city was under siege and they were at great risk of being killed by indiscriminate shelling or sniping. Were some also killed by Caco and other similar people? I would say yes. And I would say not only was Mr. Milosevic wrong when he said it was 8 or 9.000 and you were wrong when you put 2 or 3.000; I would say that Caco's victims in the Kazani pits would certainly be less than 100. Now, as for -- as for your last question, yes, I was very aware of the detainees, the Serb detainees held at the Tarcin grain silos, and there were over a hundred of them, and we protested regularly to the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was holding them illegally, in our view, until they got information about the Muslim men in Hadzici who later turned out to have been killed. But the people in that silo in Tarcin, although it was certainly a wrong thing to do, they were not -- they were not indiscriminately killed; they were not killed at all. They were simply held when they should not be held. And although that was terrible, it's quite a different order of crime, of problem, to the one we're talking about in this case, the random bombardment of a city of a quarter of a million people. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you haven't answered.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me if I was aware, and I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, in your statement you said that the people from the silos were used to clear minefields and pitfalls and to dig trenches, and that oftentimes they were killed. Is that true, concerning those people from silos, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These are your very own words.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me clear that we're talking about less than ten people, whereas in the indiscriminate bombing and shelling and sniping of Sarajevo, we're talking about the deaths of thousands and thousands of people. But yes, I'm aware of silos --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland. Your cross-examination is complete. Mr. Waespi, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just one issue the Defence might want to clear. The last document they put to the witness was the UNPROFOR report from the 29th August 1995, which is 65 ter number 481, and I suggest that it might be moved also into evidence, if Defence counsel wants to do that. That's just the last document which was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, if you wish that document to be admitted, then we'll admit it. Please give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be admitted as Exhibit D10, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I first want to clear up a couple of things which were raised today and then we'll move to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it shouldn't take that long, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The first point, Mr. Harland, you were asked in the beginning line 4 about the general assumption that sniping or shelling of civilians within the confrontation lines generally was sourced from outside the confrontation line, and it was discussed about the perception of the media as well. And your response was: "Yes," and I quote you, "not always but usually" that was the case. Can you again tell us what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The overwhelming majority of the shells that landed on Bosnian-controlled territory, that is, in the city of Sarajevo or the overwhelming majority of people who were killed by sniper fire on Bosnian-held territory of whatever nationality, those shells came from the Serb side and those bullets came from the Serb side. I would say that the number of cases in which there is serious reason to believe that people killed on the Bosnian side of the line were being killed by fire that originated on the Bosnian side of the line would probably be less than 1 per cent of the total cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland. The next document I would like to show you is Defence Exhibit number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's a document dated 1st December 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I just want to ask you one point about an answer you wanted to give about the Sagger missiles and you were sort of cut off. While the document is being retrieved at page 3, at the bottom, can you tell the Trial Chamber what Sagger missiles were -- that were fired into the city on that day?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I don't have that document in front of me but I remember the incident. The Sagger is a small wire-guided missile that operates at relatively short range, and at some point - I can't remember exactly when; later in the war - the Serbs began -- we could identify the firing point very easily, began to fire these missiles into the city of Sarajevo. And they were very easy to see where they came from because they trailed little wires behind them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know what these weapons are used for normally, what their prime military purpose is?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think in a real war they're for trying to take out armoured vehicles, but here they were just -- you know, they were fired against apartment blocks and office blocks and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the completion of the record, can you please move the document down to the bottom. And now, Your Honours, you see the reference. Sector Sarajevo, paragraph number 2, and then little (a), "380 Sagger missiles were fired into the city at lunchtime," and at the end you see that "three civilians were wounded."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move on to the next document, if I may, and this is D9, Defence Exhibit 9, dated 24th June 1995. You were asked a number of issues about this document and also the fact that the Bosnians actually launched an offensive. Please have a look at the first page of this document D9, and perhaps you can also explain the way these documents are written. I believe the front page has the highlights and list in paragraphs what is later described in detail. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and it is correct that this document referred to a Bosnian offensive out of the city. But I think the point I was trying to make in the document was that the Bosnian offensive was principally of a military nature. It was a failure, but it was directed at the Serb military. Whereas what concerned us at the time was that the Serbs then responded with an indiscriminate bombardment of the city and an increase of sniping against civilians, as the documents state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. What I also would like to ask you to look at is paragraph 3 on this cover page, the humanitarian situation. What was the humanitarian situation at that time when the Bosnian military tried to break out of the city, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was extremely bad. And whenever the Bosnians would try any sort of military activity, the Serbs would retaliate against the city as a whole and the civilian population by cutting off the electricity or limiting the amount of water or, in particular, stopping convoys of food or increasing their bombardment of civilian areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know why the Bosnian military tried to break out of the city, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the city was under siege and enduring an appalling humanitarian and general situation. The life was intolerable and they were trying to break the siege, but they failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And a related document just states a few days later, 2nd July, 1995; it's Prosecution Exhibit number 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, you heard the Defence saying it is a very important document for the Defence, and I would like to ask the witness to have a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's P19, 2nd July 1995, and we have gone over that for a while. But just have a look at it again, especially on paragraph -- on page 2, the second part of the page. "Shelling of the city, active snipers, civilian casualties." Is that an example of the point you just made a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's an example of that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And on the next page, on the top of page 3 -- in fact, that's what we had discussed yesterday, the incident about the little boy. And in fact the first sentence, and you can read it yourself, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sniper activity had spread to a number of areas usually considered reasonably safe. On Sunday, a 16-year-old boy was killed while riding his bicycle on Tito Street near UNPROFOR headquarters. Later in the week, sniping spread to the old town in the east and to the west. As with the shelling, many of the victims seem to have been hit while collecting water."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that was the situation when the Bosnian Muslims tried to break out of the city.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The retaliation was principally against civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now I would like to clear up just a few matters from yesterday, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The first one relates to the issue of the military hospitals in Lukavica. There were two instances where you weren't allowed to answer or to complete your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, it's on page 372 and 373 of yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You were asked whether you were aware of the fact that there was a hospital there for the Serbs - and that's Lukavica - and did you know that the hospital was unable to provide medical care for people who were seriously injured. And then you started your answer by saying: "Yes, and in fact the people in Lukavica used other medical facilities; that is correct" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've never said that it was at Lukavica. I said it was at Ilidza, and it's a quite a different location, at Blazuj. It's 2 or 3 kilometres away and could not have been reached from Lukavica at all. The problem was when one had to reach Lukavica from Zuja. And I never said that there was a hospital at Lukavica. There are a number of hospitals, but the hospital I mentioned was the one at Blazuj, at Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm grateful for that clarification. I'm just reading from the transcript of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: "Between Lukavica and Ilidza" was the exact quote. In any event, you start to say that "the people in Lukavica used other medical facilities; that is correct," you said yesterday, "which is not at all to say that their medical facilities were," and you couldn't answer, you couldn't continue your question. Do you have any comments about these medical facilities the Serbs used?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would only say that the Serbs would often raise concerns like this to us, like how long it took them to get to a hospital or inadequate facilities at a hospital. But, in fact, whenever there was any real comparison, the hospitals on the Bosnian side were vastly worse. And the Serbs actively cut off even the electricity and the water that might have been needed for the proper functioning of those hospitals. So I didn't want to deny that the Serbs had problems with their medical facilities, but they were vastly less than the problems they inflicted on the people who needed medical services on the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland. The next point I would like to clarify is on page 393 at the end, and it deals with the signing of the anti-sniping agreement. And you were asked by Mr. Tapuskovic that -- in fact, it was kind of a statement, that -- and I quote Mr. Tapuskovic: "Mr. Milosevic signed the agreement, in spite of all the previous obstruction. This is precisely what I wanted to hear, whether this was true." And then you are recorded as saying yes. Now, you told Your Honours yesterday who was present at that meeting where the agreement was signed. General Tolimir; it was, I think, Professor Koljevic; General Milosevic. Now, can you tell Your Honours - and you were there - what the dynamics were between those three gentlemen, especially between General Tolimir and General Milosevic, as to who is signing the agreement.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General Milosevic signed it, though it is certainly true that General Tolimir was an active agent in the process. And, in fact, he had been a strong -- General Tolimir had been a strong participant in the discussions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I must ask you to be silent, and it's a question of respect for counsel who is asking a question. If you have a matter to raise, then raise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Mr. President. Mr. Milosevic wanted to tell me something out loud, and I wanted to merely tell him that while we are in session he should not be saying anything out loud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The practice is for an accused to send a note with the security officer to counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I told him. I told him so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So he may do that. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, if you would like to complete your answer.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir was there and was a very forceful negotiator, and the position represented by all of our Serb interlocutors was that they would not accept the position which we proposed which would make it impossible to snipe, which is that line-of-sight barriers be established and that we be given authority to hunt down snipers trying to violate it. And the agreement was signed by General Milosevic when we withdrew that and accepted that they would simply make public announcements that they had agreed to stop sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just following on, that was the reason why the Bosnian Serbs actually signed this agreement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We believe -- it -- we believe that they signed it when we stopped insisting on the line-of-sight barriers or on the authority for us to go and hunt down the offending snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next point of clarification can be found on page 396 at the bottom, and Mr. Tapuskovic ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic quoted from a -- from your witness statement, and I think the quote is not entirely accurate. It is about command and control in sniping situations. And I would just like to direct you to your witness statement on page 11. That's at the bottom of page 11. And the quote you made there is as follows, and I quote: "The agreement worked well for a period in the first couple of months where sniping was quite rare. There was little doubt regarding the command and control of the warring factions over their snipers. The only doubt was sometimes that the French were not sure if shots fired at a long distance at Bosniak civilians sometimes came from the Bosniaks instead of the Serbs." Because you were quoted as saying that you had some doubts about command and control, so, Mr. Harland, can you confirm the witness statement stating that you had little doubt about command and control over snipers?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had little doubt about the command and control over snipers, and when the agreement was signed, it was then followed by a sharp reduction in the number of sniper attacks, which seemed to confirm our belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next point, second-to-last, I would like to raise with you is at page 399 and 400 of yesterday's transcript. You might recall, Mr. Harland, that you were asked about an issue involving French anti-sniping teams. And you said that the French teams had identified the firing point and they were able to point the firing point out to you. And then I quote you, saying: "And those firing points were certainly within Bosnian government-held territory, and then I was able to see for myself that sniper fire was opened from one of those positions ..." And you continue, saying that it caused "a few civilian pedestrians to run quickly for hiding ..." Now, do you recall the time of that moment when you went to see these French anti-sniping teams and they pointed out one of these Bosnian sniper locations?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time of day?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No. The time in the year. In which year and which month?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1993. Yeah, I remember. People were wearing light clothing, so I guess it was probably -- I don't know, I would guess September of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the last point, Mr. President, Your Honours, is the issue of the two Serbian girls that were sniped at, and Judge Mindua was specifically interested in this point, as we are, Mr. President. And we were able to find three documents that relate to this incident. There was an uncertainty about whether it was March 19 -- whether it was August 1994 or March 1995. I would like Mr. Harland to be shown three documents. The first one is 65 ter number 02822, and it's a document from Mr. Akashi dated 12th March 1995. It reports about meetings with Bosnian government officials. And the first paragraph is the most important, especially line 5. "My arrival in Sarajevo at 1000 this morning ..." line 5, if that could be highlighted. And I can read it for everybody's benefit. Mr. Akashi says: "My arrival in Sarajevo at 1000 hours this morning was marked by the apparent killing of two young girls - initial reports say 9 and 11 - by sniper fire in Serb-controlled Sarajevo. The closer of the Blue Routes across the Sarajevo airport by the Bosnian Serbs, which they say is in response to the killing of the two girls, by the shelling last night of down-town Sarajevo with heavy weapons - initial reports say 13 rounds of 120-millimetre mortars - and by the fact that my aircraft was hit by machine-gun fire as it taxied after landing in Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Does that refresh your memory, Mr. Harland, as to the killing of these two Serbian girls and the response of the Bosnian Serbs to that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The incident did, indeed, occur, as I think Mr. Tapuskovic said, in March of 1995. And yes, I now recall that it was repeatedly raised with us by the Serb authorities as the reason they were closing the Blue Routes and taking a number of other measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- remind us again of the importance of the Blue Routes for the population of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The so-called Blue Routes were some routes that were established to allow civilians to move between different Serb-held areas and between different Bosnian-held areas and even between some Serb- and Bosnian-held areas. And these had been negotiated originally, I think, in early 1994, and then were closed by the Serbs, I think, early in 1995, at roughly the same time they closed down the Sarajevo humanitarian air-lift that we were operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if we could move to page 2 of the same document, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Harland, who Mr. Muratovic was who met with Mr. Akashi on that day?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Muratovic was a Bosnian government minister. I think he was not yet the prime minister, but later on he was the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I direct you to the first five lines under Sarajevo, and I read it out: "Muratovic condemned the killing of the two young girls, the bodies of whom were shown in graphic detail on Bosnian Serb television last night; said that his government his formed a commission to investigate the incident but asserted that such an incident was justification for neither the shelling of Sarajevo last night nor the closure of the Blue Routes."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you also confirm, as far as you know, what Mr. Akashi says here?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the -- that was the -- that was the events, as we understood it from -- from our meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could have a number for that document. The Prosecution would like to move that into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P24, Your Honours. Also, while I'm on my feet, Your Honours, a point of clarification regarding the document with the 65 ter number 02471. That's the sitrep dated 24th of June 1995. That was tendered by the Defence and it was assigned an exhibit number of D9; however, this document was tendered and admitted yesterday by the Prosecution as Exhibit P16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next document deals with the same issue, and it's very brief, Mr. President. It's ter number 0281, and it's again a cable from Mr. Akashi dated 17th March 1995. And the previous document was a meeting between Mr. Akashi and the Bosnian government, and now it's a meeting with Mr. Karadzic. And I would like to show the witness page 4 of this document, which is actually page 3 of the actual report. And it's just one line in the middle of -- I'm not entirely sure that this is the right document. Can we see the cover page, please. I apologise, Mr. President, for these technical problems. No, it's a document -- it should be the 17th March, 1995. But if you don't have it, I can move on. Ter number 02821.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document that's on the screen is the document that we have for that 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, if, just as an emergency procedure, I could put the document onto the ELMO. I just have one copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you could show it to the Defence. It has been disclosed to the Defence, but just for transparency. That's the only copy I have, so I'm just asking the witness to quickly look at the cover page, the first page, and then the fourth page which deals with the meeting with Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's the marked portion I would like to read out. "Karadzic was adamant that the airport routes would remain closed for 60 days; 30 days for the death of each of the two killed girls in Grbavica." Do you remember these events, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a -- that was their position, and in fact I think they stayed -- stayed closed for longer than that. Yes, that was the message they passed to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to move this document into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P25, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the last document is ter number 02820, which is a daily news report dated March 15, 2006. And we're only concerned with the cover page. That's the way it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we can move down to the bottom on the left side. Yes. Bosnian Radio Sarajevo. And I'll just read out what it says, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: "Bosnian Radio Sarajevo, on Monday, reported that the General Staff of the Bosnian army officially confirmed on Monday that a Muslim sniper/shooter killed two Serb girls in Serb-controlled Grbavica near Sarajevo on Saturday. News agencies report. The Bosnian army General Staff said this was an 'accident' and added that the soldier who had killed the girls had been arrested and would stand trial." And then just to continue on top of next page. "Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic ordered Serb forces to close the 'Blue Routes' near Sarajevo because of the incident." My question is: Is that an appropriate reaction from the Bosnian Serb army, as stated here?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't consider --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you mean by "appropriate"? What do you mean by, "is that an appropriate reaction?"

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The investigation into the incident, as stated here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not clear to me how he can comment on that. Don't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's fine. That's my last question, Mr. President. And I would like to have the document moved as well into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P26, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, do you have a point?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this should not be admitted as an exhibit because we can't see that the Bosnian army has really instituted the proceedings the way they should be. This is something stated in the press, but we don't have enough evidence that indeed the proceedings were instituted or who was behind that and that criminal responsibility was indeed incurred. The fact that the media reported that somebody reacted from the Bosnian leadership is quite one matter, and quite another is to have a piece of information attesting to the fact that the person was arrested and that criminal proceedings were instituted against the person. This was not proven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I entirely agree with Mr. Tapuskovic. That's a media report and it says what it says. And that's as far as this document goes and it's up to Your Honours to consider what it says. If any party wants to take the issue further and call the people who were actually involved in investigating, then it's up to the parties. But the document addresses exactly the issue we were discussing yesterday, the killing of the two Serb girls, and I think it's perfectly valid to have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the point that you have raised doesn't affect the admissibility of the document. It goes to the weight which the Chamber will attach to it, and so it remains admitted. Mr. Harland, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I might be excused myself, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- because the next witness will be led by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. President, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood correctly, the next witness is going to come into the courtroom now. We said that there were a few procedural questions that had to be settled before the new witness. We thought that we had some procedure to settle before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long will these procedural issues take, in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at the transcript, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long will these procedural issues take, in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Tapuskovic and myself have agreed, he needs two to three minutes -- three to four minutes and I need the same, so maybe ten minutes altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll deal with the procedural matters now and then we'll have the witness afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already talked to the Prosecutor about these matters yesterday and announced that I would raise these procedural matters. We didn't have time to discuss them before. This is the point: At which point in time do the exhibits related to cross-examination have to be delivered? Different Trial Chambers have different positions on this matter. I would first wish to refer you to the decision upon joint motion by Defence on the presentation of evidence in the case IT-05-87-T, Prosecutor versus Milan Milutinovic. In this case, the Defence insisted on the right of the accused based on Article 21 because the effect of cross-examination is completely neutralised or defeated in terms of checking the credibility of the witness because it allows the Prosecution to instruct their witnesses accordingly before examination. The Trial Chamber examined the motion, and the Defence asked that the deadline within which the disclosure of material concerning cross-examination should be just immediately before the witness takes the stand and before he is directly or she is directly examined. The general position of the Prosecution is that it does not intend to oppose such a request. Three days before the current witness or the witness who just left was examined, we delivered a great volume of evidence that I selected meticulously for that particular reason. The Prosecution was able to discuss the evidence with the witness for three days, and of course the situation resulted in the conflicts or misunderstandings that we witnessed. At any rate, if, three days ahead of the witness's examination, we were to disclose the material that we would use, these three days could gravely prejudice the Defence and the accused, as was detailed -- as is provided by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, namely, Rules 54, 85, and 90. However, since the Prosecution does not challenge our motion but supports it and asks that the following paragraph replace paragraph 3 in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and it says: "The list of documents to be used in a side in cross-examination of a side of a witness must be disclosed to the other side or sides at the start of cross-examination of that witness." I don't wish to go on reading through to the end. The earlier witness showed to me that this indeed is a matter requires consideration because the time-limit of three days ahead of the witness taking the stand - and this will also apply to our witnesses when they will appear before the Court - could indeed, as detailed by the Defence counsel in that other case, prejudice and endanger the importance of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The decision in the Milutinovic case that the material concerning cross-examination should be delivered immediately before the witness takes the stand, was that specifically related to

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. And the Prosecution agreed with this. The Prosecution agreed with the motion. As soon as the witness takes the oath --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I'm asking: Does that apply for both -- did that decision relate both to Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To both parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I didn't make it quite clear. That was the first thing. And I think that the Chamber should respectfully rule on this as well. Secondly, I would like to raise the issue, a completely different issue. I believed - and this is something that you should be ruling on - that there will be enough time, but then I realised that it's going to be very difficult to find a day in a week when we can communicate between ourselves and when we can receive suggestions from the accused. It is practically very difficult during a working day and the next day to communicate with an accused and to have all this basic communication in order to receive suggestions from his side. If we had sittings every day and we cannot visit the accused on weekends, then it's going to be very difficult to establish these communications, which is sine qua non. I apologise for the suggestions that occurred a while ago, if you perceive this as contempt of court. I had to turn towards the accused. I heard what he was suggesting, but I realised that it was something up to me to prove rather than intervene on the spot in the courtroom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Generally, Mr. Tapuskovic, we are due to sit for once -- for a session from either 9.00 to 1.45 or 2.15 to 7.00, so that there would be some time for you communicate with your client. We are not sitting all day, generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is barely to maintain the communication, because I believe that in such a complex case, we can have valuable and good contacts with him and to prepare ourselves for the witnesses that are going to appear in view of the deadlines that have been set up. And I suppose that you should rule on this. And it seems to me that this motion is warranted on our side in order to enable us to maintain the minimum of fairness of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what is it that you're asking? What is it that you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are asking for one day in a week that the Chamber does not sit so that we have -- can have full contact with the accused and so that we can make all the preparations with him and receive all the suggestions from him in order for us to be able to do our job properly and prepare our Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That would be unprecedented, as far as I'm aware, that a Chamber would decide not to sit one day per week simply to allow communication between Defence counsel and his client.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there were such cases. I cannot respond to you immediately, because I was very busy preparing for this trial, but I can look at the case law of this Tribunal. Of course, Your Honours, you are directing these proceedings. You take due care of everything, and it is our duty to comply with any ruling of yours. But I do believe that this case deserves a little more time than has been allocated for the whole procedure. We do need some time. If we go on at this pace and in this manner, I'm sure that his right to a fair trial will be infringed upon. Of course, that is my opinion, and I have never claimed to always be a hundred per cent sure about any matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, you respond to the first point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will respond to the first point. Just three things to say about that. The first is that I would not share Mr. Tapuskovic's characterisation in any way with what occurred with the last witness and problems which may have arisen. But having said that, we would not object to a change in the rule that would require disclosure of cross-examination documents at the beginning of the direct examination of the witness, which is I believe what Mr. Tapuskovic is asking for. In any event, it would take care of the problem which he identified, which his concerns seem to be that the Prosecution would have an opportunity to show the documents to the witness before he testified. If we only received them when the witness begins testifying, of course that will not occur. I'll even go further and say that we, of course, would like that to be the rule. If, in the event of the -- if in -- it occurs that during the direct examination there is another document that occurs to Defence counsel that they would like to use in their cross-examination, we will generally not object to Defence counsel supplementing their list and adding that if, in fairness, that is required and it is looked on, obviously, in good faith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Milutinovic Trial Chamber's decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I am not, Your Honour. I am afraid I'm not. But I do know that there have been different practices adopted in different cases on this rule. And I certainly appreciate -- I appreciate Defence counsel's position, and, of course, I can say my generosity, in all frankness, is a little bit self-interested because I'm looking ahead to when we're going to -- the sides will be switched and the rule will be on us. And I know particularly when we're responding to a Defence case, we often have less time to respond because we get the notice with much less time - we usually only have a few days - and so we will also need the same rule when we are responding to the Defence case. So I think it's a fair rule for both sides that the disclosure occur at the beginning of the direct examination with limited and fair opportunities to supplement the list, if the need should arise. I can say one other -- one thing about the second issue, if Your Honours wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The only -- what I -- I suppose I would say two things. The first is I do believe there is a precedent for this. I think in the Prlic case, it's my understanding - and this is just based on discussions in the hall, and I may be wrong about this and it may be an incomplete understanding - but it's my understanding that one of the reasons that case sits only four days a week is precisely to allow the Defence counsel to consult with their clients. Having said that, however, I don't think that there is a basis for it in this case. I think the issues -- that the case does have some complexities, but I think the issues are relatively -- are straightforward enough and have been identified that we should be able to sit five days a week. So we would oppose a move to a four-day-a-week sitting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For that reason at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll now take the break. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. The Chamber will consider both --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think we have French on the English channel, so that's making a mess, probably, of the transcript. So we need to fix that, and I don't know if the transcript captured everything that -- yes, the transcript did not capture anything that was said because it was French coming in. So I think we need to repeat everything that just happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I see. It's not there at all. What I said was that the Chamber has heard the submissions by both parties on the questions raised by Mr. Tapuskovic and we'll give a decision shortly. So the next witness will be led my Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit. And you may begin, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Just prior to beginning questioning, I think I should indicate, for the purposes of our colleagues in the translation booth, as well as this Chamber, Lieutenant-Colonel Fortin, being Quebecois, French Canadian, prefers to testify -- will be testifying in two languages, in English during his examination-in-chief, and he prefers to respond to his cross-examination in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, could you please state your name for the proceedings and for the record.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Louis Fortin.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are kindly asking the speakers to pause between questions and answers because we need to interpret what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I did. Unfortunately, my earphones have a terrific echo so I've got them around my neck, and I didn't quite hear it in time. Could we bring PT number 2817 on the monitor in front of the witness, please. That would be his statement taken 22 November 1997, which was the subject of the Prosecution's motion and subsequent ruling under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 2817. If it helps, ERN number 00555105.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Fortin, prior to coming to testify here today, have you had an opportunity to review your written statement, which now appears on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on review of the document, I understand you wish to make only one small correction on the record, and that was with respect to paragraph 75 that appears on page 14 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for everyone's assistance, the first sentence of that paragraph presently reads: "At 8.30 the morning of June 28th, the Bosnian Serb army started shelling Stup and Nedzarici." And the correction you wish to make today is that it shouldn't read "Bosnian Serb army" but "Bosnian army." Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now -- thank you. With this correction, Lieutenant-Colonel, do you find this written statement to be true, to the best of your recollection, an accurate reflection of what you would say today if more fully examined?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With that, Your Honours, I'd ask that this be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it. Let it be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P27, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, I'm going to ask you a number of clarifying questions about this previous statement and put to you some documents which relate to the matters discussed in your statement, but before we do that, could you just tell us: Do you still hold the rank of lieutenant-colonel with the Canadian forces?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What's your present occupation?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm currently the J9 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are again kindly asking you to make pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Lieutenant, you must observe a pause between question and answer for the benefit of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Understood. I'm currently the J9 at Joint Task Force Headquarters East, one of such -- one of four such headquarters stationed in Montreal, and I'm responsible for inter-agency relations with the police, emergency services, to coordinate our response in case of domestic operations, be they earthquake, terrorist attack, or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification and additional information. Now, if we could go directly to your statement, I'd like to bring you to paragraph 13, page number 4. Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, in this paragraph you indicated your first sector commander was French General Herve Gobilliard. Do you know how long General Gobilliard had been in place by the time you arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes. General Gobilliard had been in Sarajevo for about nine months.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could move further on to paragraph 21 of your statement; that's on page 5. In paragraph 21, you generally identified who, within the sector, was responsible for liaison, but it's not clear from this paragraph whether the Serb side designated an officer responsible for dealing with UNPROFOR. Did they do that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: My understanding is that before my arrival, the Serb side also had a liaison officer in the PTT building, but when I arrived it was no longer the case. But they had designated a liaison officer who was Lieutenant-Colonel Indic, stationed in Lukavica barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if he was stationed in Lukavica barracks, in the sector, as is set out in your statement, at the PTT building in the city centre, could you tell me how sector commands liaison with the Serb side was actually carried out? How did you communicate?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: There were three ways, mainly: By phone, by fax, or through the use of a French liaison officer who was in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would that be a French UNPROFOR liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Permanently stationed in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure if he was permanently stationed there, but he was designated to work from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were there also, for example, runners who might have gone from sector headquarters to Lukavica to effect liaison?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: When necessary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall how often "necessary" might have been? Was that a daily matter, a weekly matter, or something less frequent?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, I don't recall, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps we could then just move on to paragraphs 32 and 33 of your previous statement, and those take us to page 7. Now, in those two paragraphs, you deal with correspondence received and generated by the sector command, in particular letters of protest. And maybe we could just talk briefly about those. In paragraph 32, you explain that many letters of protest were drafted by Colonel Meille. Could you -- are you aware on what information the protest was based?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Whenever there was an incident, someone broke the cease-fire - we had information from the observation posts that we had all around the city - they reported to the sector headquarters, the operations room. And based on the information we got there, we would write a letter of protest if the cease-fire was broken.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your role in the preparation of these letters was generally translations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I wrote some of them, but mostly it translated what Colonel Meille wrote in French into English. Sometimes editing was suggesting ways of phrasing the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, when the subject of the protest concerned Sarajevo and what was going on within the city, is there one individual to whom the protests were generally addressed?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: If the letter was intended to the Serb side, it would be addressed to the Serb commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And similarly, to the Bosnian side, it would go to the corps commander there?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, General Aznadzic, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, would such letters or other correspondence sometimes be signed by the sector commander in your presence?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Sometimes he would sign in front of me, yes. But usually, without being always present when he signed, I would bring in the document unsigned and then go and take it a few minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Having said that, then, perhaps we could ask you to look at a series of letters, the first bearing the PT number 2396. Wonderful. Lieutenant-Colonel, could you have a look at this letter, dated 2 June 1995 regarding access to detainees held by the Bosnian Serb forces, and tell us whether you recognise the signature on it.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, the signature of the sector commander, General Herve Gobilliard.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who is the letter addressed to?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: To General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, does this letter relate to those same UN forces described in paragraphs 50 and forward of your statement?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Can you bring the statement back, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, page number 10. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you could just scroll down to the bottom of the page so that the lieutenant-colonel can -- thank you. And perhaps we could move over to page 11.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The letter that was posted just before refers to the same presenters.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have that marked as a subsequent exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P28, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask for a further document to be brought up on the screen. It bears the PT number 2398.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, could you please have a look at this letter, dated 3 June 1995, which deals effectively with the encirclement of UNPROFOR forces by the Bosnian Serb army, and tell us who it's addressed to.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Addressed to General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we move down on the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yeah, it is that of General Gobilliard.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have that marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be admitted as Exhibit P29, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There's a further document bearing the next PT number in sequence, 2399, also dated 3 June 1995, regarding missing UNPROFOR equipment, among other things. Lieutenant-Colonel, who's this letter addressed to?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Again, to General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, that of General Gobilliard.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's also admitted. You wanted to have that admitted, I presume?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P30, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There will be three more documents of this nature, the next one being 2400, relating to the Bosnian Serb attack on Vrbanja bridge, also dated 3 June 1995. Do you -- could you tell us the addressee on the letter, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the signatory?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: General Gobilliard.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we have that marked as Exhibit P31, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P31.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: A further document bears the PT number 2401 dealing with the treatment of UNPROFOR soldiers during and following the take-over of Vrbanja and a threat to kill one of those soldiers. You see again -- you see this document now before you, Lieutenant-Colonel. Could you tell us who it's addressed to.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who is the signatory?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: General Gobilliard.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I see here that beside -- in the last paragraph of this letter, beside the name Lieutenant-Colonel Indic, who you've already mentioned and who appears further in your statement at paragraph 41, I see the name Colonel Lugonja, written here as "Lugonja". Who did you know Lugonja to be?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: My understanding is that he was a senior officer in the corps headquarters commanded by General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have that as P32, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P32.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the final document of this nature for the moment has the PT number 2413. It dates from 8 June 1995, dealing with an artillery attack by Bosnian Serb forces. Lieutenant-Colonel, does it appear on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who is the letter addressed to?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could scroll down on the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, I note the warning in the last paragraph of this letter. I wonder if you could read that to us, for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: It's General Gobilliard writing to General Milosevic. "Once more, I ask you to issue orders to prevent the situation from deteriorating to the point where a diplomatic solution is no longer possible and I bring to your attention the fact that you are responsible for the acts of the troops who implement your orders."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could have that marked as P33, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P33.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, do you recall ever having received a response to any of these letters of protest?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was it your practice to make sure that they had actually been delivered?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: We always confirmed that they had received it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How did you do that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: By phone, most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With whom?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: With Colonel Indic, or when it was hand-delivered, it was hand-delivered to him, so we knew -- we had confirmation then.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back to your statement, please, page 7, paragraph number 36. In this paragraph, Lieutenant-Colonel, you talk about your own observations of sniping. You make a number of significant comments. Perhaps I could bring you to the last sentence in paragraph 36 where you set out your assessment that "sniping in Sarajevo was used more as a terrorist tactic than anything else." Could you tell us the basis of that assessment.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Like I said in the previous sentence, "Sniping is a very efficient military tactic," meaning that usually a sniper can hold a much larger force on a stand-still for a long period of time, because every time he shows up and fires he hits an important target, a commander or something like that. In the case of the sniping that I saw in Sarajevo, the targets were not military. Sometimes they were UN soldiers; most of the time they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in this paragraph you say that you were shot at regularly on your way to the Residency. Can you remind us what's located there and why you were travelling there?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, the PTT building was in the western part of the city. The Residency was in the eastern part and it was where the BH command, or headquarters UNPROFOR, as it was what they called it, was located. And I went there regularly, almost every day, to liaise with my counterpart, the military assistant to the commander of UNPROFOR. So every evening during that period in June I would -- I would drive to the Residency to conduct my liaison.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I realise, Your Honours, that we are moving from document to document and the system seems to be working very well at this moment. I wonder if we could move to a map on the e-court; it bears the PT number 2813. Map 6 strongly resembles that map, Your Honours; however, map 6, to my knowledge, hasn't yet been uploaded into e-court. I'm in Your Honours' hands. It might be easier to have the witness refer to map number 6 on the ELMO; that would be the one, Your Honours. Perhaps you could, for the sake of technology and other things, indulge us for a moment because my colleague says the map is coming up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But because it is a map and an image it takes a bit longer to produce it than a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll wait a little.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, do you have a map from front of you on your monitor/screen?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you recognise what's depicted on the map?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: It's the city of Sarajevo with the confrontation line all around it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, I wonder if, with my colleague's assistance, you could take the marking tool on the right-hand side of your monitor and, for all of us in the courtroom, if you could point out or mark out the route that you would take from the PTT building to travel to the Presidency -- the Residency, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: The PTT building is somewhere around here. I would travel on the main route and go up, and the Residency is about here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of being sniped at while you were making that trip, which you've mentioned in your statement, could you identify what the hot spots were for you along that route, the areas of particular security concern or danger?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Actually, there were two areas, the main one being here which was called Grbavica and a Serb-held area. The last portion of the road could be observed, about that portion, from the area of Grbavica, and I was regularly getting fired at from there. What was most scary is that we knew they had heavy weapons, so small arms could not pierce my armoured vehicle but the heavy weapons could. And the other spot was right here, and it came from Bosnian -- the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, along this route, were there UNPROFOR anti-sniping posts or locations?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, mostly in that same area. From the Holiday Inn, which is about here, if I remember correctly, to here were most of the anti-sniping locations and all observing south.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the -- how did the anti-sniping post operate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were usually static vehicles with soldiers doing -- keeping observation on the area they were designated to protect from sniping, and they had orders to fire back proportionally with -- whenever they had a positive identification of a sniper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And did that work successfully?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really, Your Honour. It did offer a sense of security to the population. Soldiers were at work doing their job trying to protect them, but it was very difficult to observe snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just going back, Lieutenant-Colonel, to something you said earlier about they had heavy weapons -- it was at lines 19 through to lines 25. You know, "they had heavy weapons" and small arms couldn't pierce your armoured vehicle but heavy weapons could. When you say "they had heavy weapons," who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: The Serbs in the area of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have this image marked as the next exhibit, please, and then perhaps have a clean image of the map again on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P34.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to have the witness clarify something else from paragraph 36 on a fresh image. I think it's less confusing to have not so many markings on the map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you note also in paragraph 46 there were two or three locations where a French VAB would help people cross the street. So in regards to that paragraph I have two questions for you. First of all, could you tell us what the acronym VAB stands for? That's the first question.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: VAB means "vehicule de l'avant blinde." It's a French armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the second question is: Do you recall where these locations were where you saw the armoured vehicle helping people cross the street? And, as you're doing, can you mark it for us.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes. And from my recollection, it was in the same area near Tito barracks and near the Holiday Inn. I'm not sure which of those buildings it is, but somewhere around here, in between two areas and at those two locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, when you say "helping people cross the street," are you describing people in civilian clothing or people in military clothing? What did you observe?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, they were civilians all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we have this second image marked as P35, then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let it be so marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P35, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could return the lieutenant-colonel to his statement, paragraph 37, which appears on page 7. Sorry, it appears on page 7 at the bottom and continues on to page 8. So if you could call up page 8, the question is about -- the bottom part of the paragraph. I'm sorry, is it easier if I give you the pre-trial number of the statement each time I refer to it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a question directed to the court registrar, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 37, which is at the top of the page, you talked about a visit to a sniper nest south of Vrbanja, and finding there an underground tunnel network between buildings. The only question I ask you -- I'd like to know about that paragraph is: Can you remember approximately what time of the year this was? And it should be at the top of page 8 rather than page 9. Yeah, that's right, top of page 8, please.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: What was your question again regarding this --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you just tell us, do you remember approximately when this visit took place?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was in October.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could just scroll down the page a little bit now to paragraph 39.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You talk about something called a range card. Could you explain what that is, a range card.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, each observation post or other static UN post would basically make a drawing of its area of responsibility. So an observation post would normally be set up with a primary arc of responsibility to be observed and major features in that arc would be drawn on a range card with distance identified on the card and major features, like I said. That way it made it much faster and easier to report on things that were being observed in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, Mr. Fortin is a 92 ter witness, is he not?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, as I said in relation to the previous witness, this is an abbreviated, expedited procedure to replace examination-in-chief. I don't expect you to spend so long introducing the documents, which is really what you should be using this time for.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll take your guidance in hand, Your Honour, and move directly to the remainder of the documents that we have on our list. If I could have PT 2393 brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, in paragraph 62 of your statement you speak of a meeting between Colonel Demurenko and Indic. This document confirms -- this document talks about Colonel Demurenko confirming a letter from General Gobilliard was handed to General Milosevic. Could you please have a look at this document and tell us whether this is a report on the meeting you mention in paragraph 62.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could scroll slowly through the document for the lieutenant-colonel, I'd appreciate that. If you could continue down and then bring up the second page now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it's the letter I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have that marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P36.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honours, at this point I'd like to deal with a series of documents which I'd like to tender as contextual and illustrative of the larger context of the -- of the larger context that was in play at the time of the events the witness's statement records. And I'm in Your Honours' hands as to whether you'd like to have them brought up on the screen before we deal -- before we have them entered as exhibits, or whether I could deal with it merely orally. These, Your Honour, are generally a series of intercepted telephone communications which, in our pre-trial conference, our learned friend had conceded the authenticity of, and some documents which derive from the military archives at Banja Luka, a further collection, again, which my learned friend stated he had no objection as to the authenticity of these documents. I tender them at this point, Your Honour, purely as contextual documents that would assist Your Honours in evaluating the context of the evidence that Lieutenant-Colonel Fortin has presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Deal with the matter orally. Yes, Ms. Isailovic, I didn't see you there. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour, I have stood up to address this issue which was raised during our pre-trial conference. And if I remember correctly - and I hope this is the case - we said that we would meet to look into this question again because Mr. Tapuskovic wasn't quite sure exactly which telephone conversation you were talking about. So we had not settled the issue, and we didn't quite know which conversations we were talking about. These are telephone conversations for which we may not be able to vouch the authenticity. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I think we need to address this question and we need to meet with the Prosecution to be able to come to a solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many documents are we dealing with? How many intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please let me count for a moment, Your Honour. I counted very quickly, but I think we're dealing with a total of six or seven documents and intercepts. Could I just make the following proposal, Your Honour, that might serve to expedite things: I'd like to tender -- we're not talking, for this purpose, about exhibits that my learned friend doesn't know about, because they've already been the subject of disclosure and preparation for Lieutenant-Colonel Fortin's testimony. But nevertheless, could I suggest that they be tendered at this moment as contextual documents, and of course we will have the meeting that needs to be had in the immediate future with my learned friend, and my learned friend be given a limited period of time withing which to respond on the authenticity. And Your Honours may rule after that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, what we have in mind was instructing counsel to give you the documents immediately after we break this evening so that you can look at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, I would just like to say something. I did get three documents of this kind. I think the Prosecutor has just mentioned six documents. Did I get it wrong or did I miss something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the disclosure of documents is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You did say six? Six or seven?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, and they've been disclosed last Friday, Your Honours. So if Your Honours direct me to provide additional copies of material for the sake of clarity and expediting matters, I'm quite happy to do that. The notion behind proposing them at this moment is that it assists the parties, Your Honours and your staff included, to hear the related evidence at one time rather than diffusely through the course of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
